As vibe coding — that is, writing programs using AI prompts — becomes increasingly popular, the number of new apps submitted to the App Store has surged, doubling in the first half of 2026, yet downloads have grown by only 2%. Below is the full report.

New app submissions soar, but downloads lag far behind

The New York Times published a report today, citing the latest data from Sensor Tower, indicating that while the number of new apps submitted to the App Store doubled in the first half of 2026, downloads rose by only 2%.

The report also mentioned two developers who have been continuously releasing vibe coding apps on the App Store: Marco Pérez plans to quit his job at JPMorgan next month to devote himself full-time to app development; David Svensson, on the other hand, has launched 11 niche apps over the past five months, treating vibe coding as a hobby rather than a business.

Excerpts from the report are as follows:

Pérez, a software engineer based in Chicago, had never previously developed a mobile app. He spent five weeks during the winter researching "vibe coding" AI tools to create a prototype, followed by two weeks preparing it for submission to the App Store. His app InfoDrizzle has performed reasonably well, accumulating 1,300 downloads to date and earning approximately US$500 in profit. Pérez's next app proved even more popular. He spent roughly a week in May launching Stappa, a scrapbooking app that turns photos into digital stamps, which has since recorded 20,000 downloads and earned approximately US$3,000 in profit.

Apple spokesperson Peter Ajemian told The New York Times that the surge in submissions has brought another issue: as previously reported, the App Store's review process is under tremendous pressure.

Ajemian pointed out that "Apple has consistently been able to review 90% of app submissions within 48 hours," and added that Apple "welcomes a new generation of developers who are building and launching apps at a record pace using the latest tools."

He also emphasised that all apps "regardless of whether they were developed through vibe coding, must meet the same high standards of quality, privacy, and safety that users have always come to trust."
